FOR TRADE CONTRACTORS AND SHOP OWNERS

You do not charge what you think you charge.

A $28 wage is not a $28 hour. By the time payroll taxes, workers’ comp, the truck, the phone, the paid holidays and every hour spent driving, estimating and fixing callbacks are in it, the hour you sell costs far more — and the overhead behind it still has to come out of somewhere. Put your own year in below and see the burden rate, the overhead rate, and the number a crew hour has to be sold at.

What should I charge per hour as a contractor?

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan — what a pricebook holds, and what has to decide the number first.

This calculator vs. Housecall Pro — what a Price Book holds, and what has to decide the number first.

This calculator vs. guessing your burden and overhead — the 20%/10% rule of thumb, and what it actually costs.

The crew and the hours

The hours are the part most shops get wrong. You pay for 2,080 hours a year and you sell far fewer, and the gap has to be recovered inside the ones you do sell.

Paid days off means holidays, vacation and sick days — paid, and on nobody’s invoice. The non-billable share is everything else that is worked but not sold: drive time between jobs, loading, estimating, shop and yard time, warranty callbacks and rework. Twenty per cent is a common figure for a small crew; measure yours if you can.

What a person costs on top of the wage

Per field employee, per year. These are the costs of employing somebody rather than the costs of a job.

Workers’ comp varies more than any other figure here — a low-risk trade may be under 4% of payroll and a roofing classification many times that. Use your own declarations page, not a rule of thumb.

Overhead: the business, not the job

Annual, whole business. Anything you would still be paying in a month with no work booked.

Owner pay belongs here for the hours you spend estimating, quoting and running the shop. If you also work on the tools, count those hours in the crew above instead — splitting your own pay between the two is the most common thing to get wrong on this page. Materials and subs is your annual spend on both; it is the rest of the direct cost the overhead rate is measured against.

What you want to make

Net margin is a share of the price, not a mark-up on cost. Ten per cent margin on a $10,000 job is $1,000 of profit; a 10% mark-up on $10,000 of cost is $909. The rate you charge today is optional and changes none of the arithmetic — leave it blank and the answer is the same; fill it in and the result also says what that rate is earning, and what would have to be true for it to work.

      These four are the fields every trade bid calculator on this site asks for. Save them once and each one opens with your numbers instead of a stranger’s ballpark.

          The form opens on a worked example for a three-person crew. Change what is different about your shop and press the button.

          These are the worked example’s figures, not yours yet. Change what is different about your shop and press the button.

          Common questions

          Why does it say my payroll burden is 92% when everyone quotes 20–30%?

          Because the usual figure answers a different question. “Taxes plus insurance as a percentage of wages” is the textbook definition, and on the worked example that really is about 20%. But you pay wages on every paid hour and you invoice only some of them — 15 paid days off, and a fifth of the hours you do work going to drive time, estimating, shop time and warranty callbacks. The example pays 2,080 hours and bills 1,568. Burden here is the percentage that recovers the whole annual cost of employing someone across only the hours that get sold, which is what every bid calculator on this site multiplies by job hours. Use 20% there and the unbilled hours are never recovered on any job.

          Isn’t overhead a percentage of revenue?

          On a profit-and-loss statement, yes. Here it is deliberately a percentage of direct cost, because that is what the bid calculators do with it: they take a job’s labor plus materials and add the overhead rate on top. The denominator is annual direct cost — loaded field labor plus materials and subcontractors — so the number transfers cleanly. Mixing the two up is a quiet, consistent under-recovery on every job you price, because overhead-over-revenue is always the smaller number.

          What is the difference between the bill rate and the break-even rate?

          The break-even rate is what an hour costs you once burden and overhead are both covered — $65.18 on the worked example. Bill at exactly that and you finish the year with zero profit, having worked all of it. The bill rate adds your target net margin on top: at 12% that is $74.07. The gap between the two is the entire profit of the business, which is why a “small” discount off the bill rate is a large fraction of the margin rather than a large fraction of the price.

          Why does the non-billable percentage move the rate so much?

          Because it shrinks the denominator that everything else is divided by. It is the single most sensitive input on this page: the annual cost of employing someone does not change when utilization drops, so every unbilled hour has to be recovered by the hours that remain. The worked example bills 75% of its paid hours. If your crew is at 60% because of drive time or a long quoting cycle, the same wage and the same overheads need a materially higher rate to come out level. Be honest with this number rather than optimistic — it is the one most shops guess high on.

          What do I do with the burden and overhead numbers once I have them?

          Carry them. Every trade bid calculator on this site asks for crew wage, payroll burden %, overhead on direct cost %, and target margin, and those four are exactly what this page computes. Saving them here fills them in on the other tools so you type them once and price every job from the same business figures, instead of reaching for “about 20%” from memory on each one. If a computed rate is too large for the receiving forms to accept, the result says so rather than silently carrying a number that would be dropped.

          Do I count the owner’s pay as overhead or as crew?

          If the owner is working in the field on the jobs being priced, that time belongs in the crew wage and the crew count. If the owner is estimating, selling, and running the office, that pay is overhead — and leaving it out entirely, which is the common habit in an owner-operated shop, makes the overhead rate too low and the bill rate too low with it. Someone has to pay for the hours spent quoting the jobs you did not win, and this is the line where that happens.

          Is my data uploaded anywhere?

          No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your rates are saved in this browser’s local storage so the other tools on this site can use them and so they are still here next visit. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your wages, overheads, or the rate it works out.

          Is this an accounting or tax opinion?

          No. It is your own numbers, divided. It makes no determination about tax treatment, workers’ comp classification, or whether anyone is an employee or a contractor, and it does not tell you what to charge — the market and your own judgement do that. Check the figures against your payroll records, your insurance declarations, and a qualified professional before you price work with them.

          No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, insurance, or financial advice, and it does not tell you what to charge, what your workers’ comp classification is, or how anyone should be classified or paid. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Verify every figure against your own payroll records, insurance declarations, and accounts, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or pricing work with it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

          Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. Your wage, payroll costs, overhead and resulting rates are never uploaded and never appear in a usage count — those are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally. Saving your shop rates writes the four carried figures to this site’s own browser storage so the bid calculators can read them; clearing your browser data clears them. “Save this scenario on this device” writes all eighteen figures the same way, so you are not retyping your whole payroll and overhead picture on your next visit — deliberately local storage only, with no shareable link: a shop’s payroll and overhead are more than should ever ride in a URL you might paste into a chat app.

          Pricing custom field work instead of shop labor? The custom farm rate calculator works out a per-acre rate from a machine's field capacity, fuel, repairs, and ownership cost — nothing uploaded.

          Pricing small repair jobs rather than crew hours? The handyman minimum job calculator adds drive, estimate and supply-run time to each call and shows the smallest job worth driving to and the minimum trip charge. To price a whole job in any trade from hours, materials, subs and a target margin, use Trade Bid Studio.

          Running an auto repair shop and want to check the rate you are actually collecting rather than the one you should charge? The effective labor rate calculator takes a month you have already billed and shows what reached the invoice, split between customer-pay discounting, warranty and unbilled comebacks — the same question from the other end of the year.

          Billing someone else’s labor to a client rather than your own crew’s? The staffing markup calculator prices a placement the way agencies quote it — a markup on the pay rate — and shows what that markup earns once capped unemployment taxes, the workers’ comp class code, and the wait to be paid are counted.

          Buying leads from Thumbtack, Angi or Google Local Services? The home service lead ROI analyzer reads your lead log and shows the cost per booked job for each source — nothing uploaded.

          Towing or roadside and unsure whether a motor-club dispatch covers the truck-hour? The tow motor club call calculator turns your truck cost, deadhead and wait into profit per truck-hour and a break-even payout — nothing uploaded.

vs-guessing-your-burden-and-overhead.htm.text:
← Shop Rate Calculator

This calculator vs. guessing your burden and overhead

Most bid calculators ask for a payroll burden and an overhead rate, and most contractors answer from memory — "about 20%" and "about 10%" are the two figures that come up most. This page is about what changes when those two numbers come from your own payroll and cost records instead.

What each approach is

Guessing from memory means typing "20%" for payroll burden and "10%" for overhead into a bid calculator because those are the round numbers that circulate among contractors, without checking either against an actual year of payroll and cost records. It costs nothing and takes no time, and it is the default nearly everyone starts from — not because it is wrong on purpose, but because working out the real numbers looks like an accounting exercise most people would rather not do between bids.

This calculator takes the records a shop already keeps — wages, payroll taxes, workers' comp, liability insurance, benefits, vehicles and tools, paid and billable hours, and the fixed cost of running the business for a year — and computes the same two numbers instead of recalling them. It runs once, in the browser, on nothing that leaves the device, and it produces a break-even hourly rate and the rate a target margin actually requires, built from that shop's own year rather than a number that circulates.

The gap between the two is not rounding error. On this calculator's own shipped example — a $28 wage, three-person crew, 75% of paid hours actually billed, and a 12% target margin — the 20%/10% guess prices an hour at $42.00. The same year, run through this calculator, needs $74.07: a 92% payroll burden once the paid hours that are never billed are counted, and a 21.3% overhead rate once it is measured against direct cost the way bidding arithmetic actually uses it rather than against revenue the way a P&L states it. That is $32.07 an hour short, or roughly $150,000 a year across a three-person crew — not a number that shows up as a line on a statement, but as jobs that were priced to lose money from the day they were bid.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want an answer in ten seconds and I am not touching my payroll records right now.The 20%/10% guess — free, but built from habit, not this business's own year.
What does my payroll burden and overhead actually come out to, from my own numbers?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account, no upload.
Is a rate built on the 20%/10% guess actually covering my costs?Run the same year through this calculator and compare the two rates directly.
Which of my numbers moves the answer the most?This calculator's notes — on the shipped example it is the billable-hours share, not either guessed percentage.
How does the math behind a shop rate actually work?This calculator's own hourly-rate walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account, upload payroll data, or sign up?No, for either approach — the guess needs nothing and neither does this calculator.

The guess is not a bad habit so much as a shortcut with a real cost that stays invisible until a slow quarter or a lost bid makes it obvious. This calculator does not remove the shortcut's convenience — it is still one page, still free, still nothing to sign into — it just replaces the two recalled numbers with the two computed ones.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Why not just use 20% burden and 10% overhead like everyone says?

Because those two figures answer different questions than the ones a bid calculator needs. The textbook 20% payroll burden is employer taxes, workers' comp, and liability as a percentage of wages, and it assumes every paid hour is billed. A field employee is paid for roughly 2,080 hours a year; holidays and vacation come off that, and of the hours actually worked, drive time, loading, estimating, shop time, and warranty callbacks are on nobody's invoice. Once burden is expressed per billable hour instead of per paid hour, the same payroll can come out to 60%, 90%, or more. The textbook 10% overhead is usually a share of revenue, borrowed from a profit-and-loss statement, while bidding arithmetic applies overhead to a job's direct cost -- a smaller number, so the same dollars of rent, software, and owner pay come out to a higher percentage against it. Both guesses are round numbers pulled from habit rather than computed from either business's own records, and on the shipped example they under-price an hour by $32.07.

How much difference does it actually make?

On this calculator's own shipped example -- a $28 wage, three-person crew, 75% billable share, and a 12% target margin -- the 20%/10% guess prices the hour at $42.00. The same year's own numbers, run through this calculator, need $74.07: a 92% payroll burden once unbillable paid hours are counted, and a 21.3% overhead rate once it is measured against direct cost rather than revenue. That is $32.07 an hour short, or roughly $150,000 a year across a three-person crew before any of it shows up as a missed number on a P&L -- it shows up as work that was always going to lose money, priced as though it would not.

Where would I get the real numbers instead of guessing?

From records most shops already keep: last year's payroll (wages, employer payroll taxes, workers' comp premium, liability insurance, benefits), what was paid for vehicles, fuel, phones, and tools, and the fixed cost of running the business for a year -- owner and office pay, rent and utilities, software, marketing, and other insurance and licenses -- plus what was spent on materials and subcontractors. This calculator turns those into the payroll burden per billable hour and the overhead rate on direct cost automatically; nothing has to be looked up or estimated once the underlying figures are in hand, and nothing is uploaded anywhere to get the answer.

What if I don't know my exact billable-hours percentage?

A rough estimate is still far better than skipping the input, because it is the single figure this arithmetic is most sensitive to: on the shipped example, moving the billable share by ten points changes the required rate by more than the entire target margin does. A shop with no time-tracking can start from paid hours minus holidays, vacation, and a rough guess at drive time and shop time, see the rate that guess implies, and tighten the estimate later -- which is still a computed number checked against a business's own year, not a round figure recalled from habit.

Is this the same as reading a P&L or asking a bookkeeper?

No, and it does not replace either. A profit-and-loss statement reports what already happened, expressed as percentages of revenue; a bookkeeper or accountant can confirm the underlying payroll and cost figures are correct. This calculator does the one piece neither of those hands over on its own: converting a year of payroll and overhead into a burden rate per billable hour and an overhead rate on direct cost, in the form a bid calculator actually consumes. It is arithmetic on numbers a contractor supplies, not an accounting or tax determination.

Open the Shop Rate Calculator to work out your own rate.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or fire-safety advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, and supply costs before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device; this page names no company and compares against a generic pricing habit, not a product.

Free and open source. If it wins you a job, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-housecall-pro.html.text:
← Shop Rate Calculator

This calculator vs. Housecall Pro

Two different questions: Housecall Pro is account-based field-service software for running a trade business, and its Price Book is where prices live once they are decided. This page is a free, private worksheet for the question that comes first — what does one billable crew hour actually cost you?

What each tool is for

Housecall Pro is field service management software for home service businesses, sold as an ongoing subscription account. It covers online booking, scheduling and dispatch, automated customer texts, a mobile app that lets a crew pull up the work order in the field, estimates and invoicing with automated payment reminders, card payments, and a Price Book that holds the prices and rates a business quotes from — a system meant to run a whole company across every technician and every job. It publishes that it is used by over 200,000 field service professionals across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, cleaning, and other trades. Housecall Pro's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field-service management software for trade contractors, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Housecall Pro appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Housecall Pro does. It does not book a job, dispatch a crew, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes your own annual figures — payroll, paid and billable hours, crew size, vehicles, insurance, rent and office cost, materials and subcontractor spend — and turns them into four numbers about your business rather than about any one job: the payroll burden per billable hour, the overhead rate as a percentage of direct cost, the break-even hourly rate, and the rate a target net margin actually requires.

It also runs the arithmetic backwards, which is the direction most contractors actually need. Enter the rate you charge today and it solves for the net margin that rate really earns, the annual size of the gap across your crew — stated over labour revenue only, since materials and subs are billed on top of the hours rather than through the rate — and the billable hours that rate would need in order to work. When the hours it would require exceed the hours anyone actually works, the answer is that no schedule saves the rate.

The two are complementary rather than alternatives, and the relationship is one-directional: something has to decide the number that goes into a price book, and a price book does not derive that number from your payroll. The output here is an hourly rate and an overhead percentage you can type into whichever system quotes from them.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Housecall Pro?

They answer different questions, and a growing trade contractor will likely end up touching both. Housecall Pro is field service management software for home service businesses, sold as an ongoing subscription account, covering areas such as online booking, scheduling and dispatch, a mobile app for the crew in the field, estimates and invoicing, card payments, and a Price Book that holds the prices and rates a business quotes from. It publishes that it is used by over 200,000 field service professionals across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, cleaning, and other trades. Housecall Pro's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field-service management software for trade contractors, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Housecall Pro appears on this page. This calculator does one narrower thing, and it sits upstream of a price book rather than replacing one: from your own annual payroll, paid and billable hours, vehicles, insurance, rent, office cost, materials and subcontractor spend, it works out the payroll burden per billable hour, the overhead rate as a percentage of direct cost, the break-even hourly rate, and the rate a target net margin actually requires. It will also take the rate you charge today and solve backwards for the net margin that rate really earns, the annual size of the gap across your crew, and the billable hours that rate would need in order to work. A contractor who needs online booking, dispatch, invoicing, and payments across every technician and every job is better served by Housecall Pro or a comparable field-service platform; a contractor who wants to know what number belongs in a price book in the first place, privately and without an account, is in the right place here.

Does a Price Book not already tell me my rate?

A price book stores and applies the price you decided on; it does not derive it from your payroll. Whatever system holds your prices — Housecall Pro's Price Book, a spreadsheet, or a laminated card in the van — something has to decide the number that goes in, and that decision is arithmetic about your business rather than about any one job. This calculator is that arithmetic. It is also why the two are complementary rather than alternatives: the output here is an hourly rate and an overhead percentage you can type into whichever system quotes from them.

Why does this calculator say my payroll burden is far above 20%?

Because it counts the paid hours you never bill. The textbook burden figure — employer taxes, workers' compensation, and liability expressed as a percentage of wages — lands near 20% and assumes every paid hour is sold. A field employee is paid for roughly 2,080 hours a year; holidays and vacation come off that, and of the hours actually worked, drive time, loading, estimating, shop time, and warranty callbacks appear on nobody's invoice. Bid calculators multiply a loaded wage by the hours estimated for a job, which are billable hours, so the rate they need is the one that recovers a person's whole annual cost across only the hours that get sold. On this tool's shipped example that turns a 28-dollar wage into 53.76 per billable hour — a 92% burden, not 20%. Using 20% under-recovers labour on every job in the same direction.

Which input changes the answer most?

The billable share — the fraction of paid hours that actually get sold. In this arithmetic ten points of utilization moves the required rate further than the entire target margin does, which is the argument for measuring it rather than estimating it, and it is why the tool's notes call it out when it falls below 60%. That sensitivity is also why a rate that looks survivable can stop working after a slow quarter without any wage or overhead changing.

Is this page affiliated with Housecall Pro?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Housecall Pro. Housecall Pro is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, and supply costs before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against Housecall Pro — it is a static page describing publicly documented facts.

Which input changes the answer most?

The billable share — the fraction of paid hours that actually get sold. In this arithmetic ten points of utilization moves the required rate further than the entire target margin does, which is the argument for measuring it rather than estimating it, and it is why the tool's notes call it out when it falls below 60%. That sensitivity is also why a rate that looks survivable can stop working after a slow quarter without any wage or overhead changing.

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by ServiceTitan. ServiceTitan is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

Open the Shop Rate Calculator to work out your own rate.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against ServiceTitan — it is a static page describing publicly documented facts.

what-should-i-charge-per-hour.html.text:
SHOP RATE CALCULATOR

What should I charge per hour as a contractor?

There is no table that answers this, and any page that gives you one is guessing about your shop. What there is, is a way to work it out from four things you already know: what you pay, what employing somebody costs on top of that, what the business costs to run, and how many of the hours you pay for you actually get to sell.

Work out my shop rate →

A $28 wage is not a $28 hour

Take a three-person crew paid $28 an hour, 40 hours a week, 52 weeks, with 15 paid days off. That is 2,080 paid hours each, of which 120 are holidays and vacation. Say a fifth of the hours actually worked go on drive time, loading, estimating, and putting right the job that came back. That leaves 1,568 billable hours — a 75% billable share, which is a reasonable year, not a bad one.

Now add what that person costs beyond the wage:

Wages, 2,080 h at $28$58,240
Payroll taxes, comp and liability at 20% of wages$11,648
Benefits$4,800
Truck, fuel, phone, small tools$9,600
Cost of employing one person$84,288
Divided by 1,568 billable hours$53.76 / h

That is a 92% labor burden, not the 20–30% usually quoted. Both figures are honest; they answer different questions. Twenty per cent is taxes and insurance as a share of wages. Ninety-two per cent is what has to be added to the wage so that the hours you sell pay for the hours you don’t.

Overhead: on cost, not on revenue

Overhead is what you would still be paying next month with nothing booked — owner and office pay, the yard, software, accounting, insurance, marketing, licences. It has to be recovered through the work, and there are two ways to express it.

A profit-and-loss statement puts overhead over revenue. Bidding arithmetic — including every trade bid calculator on this site — applies an overhead rate to a job’s direct cost. The two are different numbers for the same business, and using the smaller one where the larger is wanted under-recovers overhead on every job you price.

For the crew above, with $92,000 of annual overhead and $432,864 of direct cost — three people at $84,288 plus $180,000 of materials and subs — the overhead rate on direct cost is 21.3%. Over the revenue it implies, the same overhead is about 15%.

Then, and only then, the margin

Cost per billable hour, plus overhead, gives the break-even hour: $53.76 × 1.213 = $65.18. Below that the hour loses money before anybody has been paid a profit.

Margin is taken as a share of the price, so you divide rather than multiply. At a 12% target net margin, $65.18 ÷ 0.88 = $74.07 an hour. Marking the cost up by 12% instead would give $73.00 and a margin of 10.7% — the margin-versus-markup mix-up, costing about a dollar an hour, every hour.

Which number is doing the damage

When the rate comes out higher than the market seems to bear, the instinct is to cut the margin. It is almost never the margin. In this arithmetic the sensitive number is the billable share: at 65% rather than 75%, the same crew’s break-even hour rises to about $76. Ten points of utilization moves the rate further than the entire target margin does.

That is the argument for measuring it. The rest of these inputs come off a payroll report and an insurance declarations page. The billable share is the one you have to observe, and it is the one that decides the price.

And what the rate you charge today is earning

Everything above works forwards: your year, then the rate it needs. Most contractors arrive with the answer already filled in — there is a number on last week’s quote — and the useful question runs the other way. Suppose the crew above charges $70 an hour against the $74.07 the year requires. That is not a catastrophe and it is not fine either, and the three ways of saying so are worth separating.

Charged$70.00 / h
Net margin it actually earns on labour6.9%, not 12%
Short, per billable hour$4.07
Over a year, across three crew$19,137
Billable hours that would make $70 right1,659 h (80%)

The last row is the one that is hard to get at any other way. A rate is not simply too low; it is too low given a billable share. At $70 an hour this shop would need each person to sell 1,659 hours a year — 80% of every hour it pays for, against the 75% it actually gets. Whether five points of utilization is available is a question about scheduling and estimating time, and it is a real alternative to raising the price. When the required hours come out above the hours anybody actually works, that alternative is gone and the gap is in the rate.

The calculator does this comparison from your own figures: type what you charge into the optional field, and the result says the margin it earns, the size of the gap over a year, and the billable share it would take to justify it. Leave it blank and nothing changes — it alters none of the arithmetic above.

What this page is not

This is not a price list, a wage survey, or a statement of what work is worth in your area. It is not tax, accounting, insurance, or legal advice, and it makes no determination about how anybody should be classified or paid. The percentages above are illustrative inputs, not benchmarks — workers’ compensation rates in particular vary by trade and state by more than any other figure here, and belong to your own declarations page rather than to a rule of thumb.

Put your own numbers in →

Common questions

What should I charge per hour as a contractor?

There is no table that answers this, because the number is made of your payroll, your vehicles, your overhead and the share of paid hours you actually bill. Work it as cost per billable hour, add overhead as a percentage of direct cost, then divide by one minus your target net margin. On a $28 wage with a 75% billable share, a small crew commonly lands between $65 and $95 an hour.

What is labor burden and what does it include?

Labor burden is everything you pay to employ somebody beyond the wage itself: employer payroll taxes, workers' compensation, liability insurance charged on payroll, benefits, and the truck, fuel, phone and small tools that person needs. The figure that matters for pricing also spreads paid but unbillable hours — holidays, vacation, drive time, estimating, callbacks — over only the hours you sell.

Why is my labor burden higher than 30%?

The 20–30% figure usually quoted counts only taxes and insurance as a percentage of wages. It does not account for the paid hours that are never billed. If you pay for 2,080 hours and bill 1,568 of them, a quarter of the wage bill has to be recovered inside the hours you do sell, which typically pushes the real burden past 60%.

Is overhead a percentage of revenue or of cost?

Both are used and they are not interchangeable. A profit-and-loss statement expresses overhead as a share of revenue. Bidding software, including the calculators on this site, applies an overhead rate to a job's direct cost. Using the revenue figure where the cost figure is wanted under-recovers overhead on every job.

What is the difference between margin and markup?

Margin is a share of the price; markup is added to the cost. A 10% margin on a $10,000 price is $1,000 of profit. A 10% markup on $10,000 of cost gives a $11,000 price and $1,000 of profit, which is a 9.1% margin. Quoting a margin and pricing a markup is a common and expensive mix-up.
